ABSTRACT
Excessive fossil fuel use has caused severe pollution and global warming, making the adoption of clean, efficient, 
and renewable energy essential. This study focuses on synthesizing the Ni@MCTAC nanocomposite, comprising 
multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs), activated carbon from Conocarpus tree bark (AC-CTB), and Ni 
nanoparticles, using a straightforward ultrasonic technique. Structural and morphological analyses reveal Ni and 
MWCNTs attached to the AC-CTB surface in the Ni@MCTAC nanocomposite. The Ni@MCTAC nanocomposite

1. Introduction
The increasing energy demand, and vastly depleting fossil fuels are 
the two main reasons to create the research interest towards clean, 
green, and renewable energy sources for energy production and storage. 
In the last few decades, fuel cells and batteries have played a major role 
in our earth's indispensable energy requirements but the two funda -
mental components of systems that continuously store and distribute 
energy are traditional capacitors and batteries. Batteries, on the other 
hand, provide a substantial amount of energy with low power density, 
whereas ordinary capacitors have no energy density but provide high 
power density [ 1 – 5 ]. As a result, attention to evolve the improved high- 
power, and high-energy density energy storage devices has been focused 
by many researchers [ 6 , 7 ].
Supercapacitors (SCs) are one kind of energy storage system that has 
captivated a lot of scientific interest today. Supercapacitors have two 
distinct methods of storing energy: electrical double-layer capacitance 
(EDLC) and pseudocapacitance. Carbonaceous materials with excess 
conductivity and high surface areas like activated carbon (AC), gra -
phene, and carbon nanotubes (CNTs) are known as EDLC electrode 
materials [ 8 , 9 ]. On the other side, metal oxides, carbides, nitrides, sel -
enides, and conducting polymers undergo reversible redox reactions 
which are pseudocapacitive electrode materials because of their abun -
dance in nature, cost-effectiveness, and extraordinary capacity to store

2.5. Electrochemical measurements
The electrochemical performance of the Ni@MCTAC, MCTAC, and 
AC-CTB electrodes, as well as the constructed asymmetric super -
capacitor (Ni@MCTAC//AC-CTB) was analyzed using cyclic voltam -
metry (CV), chronopotentiometry, and electrochemical impedance 
spectroscopy (EIS) experiments. The active materials (AC-CTB, MCTAC, 
and Ni@MCTAC) were mixed with the carbon black using N -methyl-2- 
pyrrolidone (NMP) solvent to prepare slurries. Without adding any 
binders, these resulting slurries were applied to the flexible carbon cloth 
current collectors. The coating area of the current collector is 1 × 1 cm
2
. 
The coated AC-CTB, MCTAC, and Ni@MCTAC electrodes were dried 
overnight inside a hot air oven. The AC-CTB, MCTAC, and Ni@MCTAC 
electrodes are employed as working electrodes, whereas Ag/AgCl and Pt 
act as the reference and counter electrodes, respectively. The aqueous 
solution of 1 M H
2
SO
4 
was employed as an electrolyte for the half-cell 
studies. In the case of the Ni@MCTAC//AC-CTB [full cell (two-elec -
trode)] configuration, the fabricated flexible Ni@MCTAC is used as the 
positive electrode, AC-CTB as the negative electrode, and PVA/H
2

2.6. Material characterization
The XRD analysis of MWCNTs, MCTAC, and Ni@MCTAC was 
examined using an accelerator detector-equipped Bruker Advanced-D8 
powder diffractometer (Cu-Ka radiation, λ = 1.5418 Å). A Labram HR 
800 Raman spectrometer was used to record the micro-Raman spectra. A 
Hitachi 3000-N Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscope (FE-SEM) 
along with Energy Dispersive X-ray (EDX) was employed to study the 
elemental compositions and surface morphology. With an accelerating 
voltage of 200 kV, Higher-Resolution Transmission Electron Microscopy 
(HR-TEM, Tecnai G2 20 S-TWIN) was employed to analyze the atomic 
structure and characteristics of the produced samples. Brunauer- 
Emmetter-Teller (BET) analyzer (Model-Autosorb IQ, Quanta chrome 
Instruments) was used to study the surface area and pore size by N
2 
gas 
adsorption-desorption isotherm experiments. Using a PHI 5000 Versa 
Probe ULVAC apparatus, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, PHI 
Quantera XPS) was used to analyze elements.
3. Results and discussion
The structural information of AC-CTB, MCTAC, and Ni@MCTAC 
nanocomposite was acquired from XRD analysis, and the results are 
shown in Fig. 1 . The distinctive peak of amorphous AC-CTB is confirmed 
by the wide peaks at 2 θ = 26
◦
and 40
◦
, respectively, that match with the 
hkl planes of (002) and (100) ( Fig. 1 a) [ 40 ]. There is a significant 
amount of disorder present, and the XRD patterns that arise are 
consistent with typical ICDD data (98 – 005-2230) [ 41 ]. In Fig. 1 b, after 
the addition of AC-CTB into MWCNTs, the XRD arrangement of MCTAC 
shows two noticeable peaks at 2 θ = 25
◦
and 42
◦
that confirm the pres -
ence of amorphous carbon amalgamation with the peaks present at 2 θ =
26
◦
and 43
◦
in the MWCNTs matrix [ 41 ]. The presence of a structured 
arrangement of carbon atoms having a greater degree of crystallinity in 
MCTAC caused the crystallinity of AC-CTB to rise after the addition of 
MWCNTs. The Ni@MCTAC nanocomposite ( Fig. 1 c) exhibited all of the 
recognizable diffraction peaks of Ni, MCTAC, and AC-CTB, appearing at 
2 θ = 26
◦
, 44
◦
, 51
◦
, and 76
◦
respectively. The (002) and (100) hkl planes 
of MCTAC are suppressed when Ni is added, while three additional hkl 
planes of Ni are promoted: (111), (200), and (220) [ 42 ]. Other than 
these peaks, no new peak was observed meaning that there is no im -
purity indeveloped Ni@MCTAC nanocomposite.
The Raman spectra of AC-CTB, MCTAC, and Ni@MCTAC nano -
composite are shown in Fig. 2 . Two prominent peaks are seen in Fig. 2
(a), and they are located at 1358 cm
� 1 
and 1597 cm

These correlate to the D-band and G-band of the AC-CTB [ 41 ]. The 
disorganized, amorphous character of carbon with deficient sites was 
connected to the D-band, whereas graphitic carbon was correlated to the 
G-band [ 43 ]. Furthermore, there was greater graphitization of AC-CTB, 
as shown by the degree of graphitization (ID/IG) of 0.85. Two distinct 
peaks could be seen in the case of MCTAC ( Fig. 2 (b)). The D band has 
one peak at around 1356 cm
� 1
, which might be caused by large flaws or 
deficiencies in the carbon nanostructures. The G band, formed through 
the tangential vibrations of carbon atoms, is attributed to the other band 
at 1598 cm
� 1

a nominal degree of defects [ 41 , 44 ]. In Ni@MCTAC ( Fig. 2 (c) ) , a new 
peak appears at 2196 cm
� 1 
alongside the characteristic bands at 1356 
and 1596 cm
� 1

nanoparticles into the MCTAC matrix [ 45 ]. The appearance of this band
